title: In dulci jubilo
description: Robert Lucas de Pearsall's setting of the old German Christmas carol, in his own words, half English and half Latin, taken from W. J. Westbrook's reduction for four voices and arranged for 2 to 4 singers. Verses 1 and 2, the carol's four-part opening, in F at a steady three beats a bar, each ending with a Latin refrain: "Alpha es et O!" and "Trahe me post te!"

credits.words: Robert Lucas de Pearsall (1837), translating the old German and Latin carol and keeping its Latin
credits.tune: "In dulci jubilo", the old German carol melody
credits.arrangement: Robert Lucas de Pearsall's setting (1837), in W. J. Westbrook's reduction for four voices, adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: Robert Lucas de Pearsall (died 5 August 1856, Wikipedia) translated the old carol's German lines into English and kept its Latin, as his preface says ("The words are rather remarkable, being written half in Latin and half in the upper German dialect. I have translated them to fit the music"); sung here as Novello's Part-Song Book No. 296 prints verses 1 and 2 under the music, spellings kept ("shew", "præsepio", "gloriæ"), the treble's punctuation given to every part; "puer", printed under one minim in verse 2, is sung "pu-er" on two crotchets in every part. Verses 3 ("O patris charitas") and 4 ("Ubi sunt gaudia"), set by Pearsall as solos for some voices answered by a chorus (pp. 84 to 88), are not sung: see the arrangement
licence.tune: public domain: the old German carol melody "In dulci jubilo", which Pearsall used as a cantus firmus; his preface says it is "to be found in an old German book published in the year 1570" (the ritual of the Protestant congregations of Zweibrücken and Neuburg), where it is called "a very ancient song (uraltes Lied), for Christmas-eve"; sung as the treble prints it, note for note
licence.arrangement: Robert Lucas de Pearsall's setting for eight voices (died 1856; his preface: written for and performed by the Choral Society at Carlsruhe), in William Joseph Westbrook's reduction for four voices (died 1894), who says in his footnote that he took "the composer's parts with as little alteration as possible"; both public domain. Sung here: verses 1 and 2, the four-part opening of the carol (pp. 82 to 84), sung twice as printed (about 2 minutes 15 seconds); the rest of the piece, verses 3 and 4, is through-composed, with solo entries and voices coming in one after another, and is left out. Pearsall's own eight-voice print could not be opened (IMSLP's download check), so his eight parts were not compared and none of them is added. Westbrook's key, tune and bass, with the inner parts revoiced for 2 to 4 beginners (beats of verse 1; verse 2 is 93 beats later). One note a syllable in the lower parts where the tune holds: the alto's passing crotchets under "ju-" and "hom-" (his F4, E4) become one F4; the tenor's B-flat3 under the held "O!" of the first refrain (his A3, B-flat3) is left out. The lower parts move under the tune's own slurs only where the chord changes: "lo", "shew", "cli-", the two "o!" and the first refrain's "O!". The alto takes the chord's third where Westbrook's alto doubles the tune, sits an octave or a fifth under it on a strong beat, or lies a second under it: A3 on the first "In" (his C4); F4, A4 on "bi- lo" and "age shew" (his D4, C4), then his F4, E4; A4, F4, E4, E4 on "Our heart's joy re-" (his F4, F4, E4, G4; his F4 on "heart's", a sixth under the tune); D4, then A3 on "neth" (his F4, F4, in unison with the tune), rising to B-flat; B-flat3, D4, C4, B-flat3 on "In præ- se- pi-" (his F4, F4, F4, E4) and A3, B-flat3, C4 in sixths under the tune's "o!" (his F4 held, in unison with it); D4, A4, G4, E4, E4, C4, D4 on "And like a bright star shi- neth" (his F4, F4, F4, E4, G4, C4, F4); A3, B-flat3, D4, C4, B-flat3 on "Ma- tris in gre- mi-" (his F4, F4, F4, F4, E4) and A3, B-flat3, C4 on "o!" (his F4 held); A3, A3, C4 on "Al- pha es" (his D4, D4, D4, in unison with the tune's low D4 and then a second under its E4), so the chord is Pearsall's D minor over F (the duet a bare fourth there, for three beats, the trio and quartet his chord), then C over E where he has E, G, D; C4, B-flat3, B-flat3, B-flat3, A3 on the second "Al- pha es et O!" (his F4, F4, F4, E4, F4). The tenor gives the alto room and keeps each chord whole: C4 on "lo" and "shew" (his A3); F3, F3, C4, C4, A3 on "Our heart's joy re- cli-" (his C4, B-flat3, G3, E3, F3 then A3), so "heart's" and "a" are his B-flat chord; F3 under "In præ- se-" and "Ma- tris in gre-" (his D4, D4, C4 and D4), so the chord is G minor seven over B-flat, E3 on "pi-" and "mi-" (his B-flat3) and F3 held through "o!" (his A3, B-flat3, C4); F3, F3, F3, C4, C4, A3 on "And like a bright star shi-" (his D4, C4, B-flat3, G3, E3, F3); F3 on "Ma-" (his A3); F3 on "Al- pha" (his A3) and F3 held on "O!" (his A3, B-flat3); A3, F3, F3, E3, F3 on the last "Al- pha es et O!" (his F3, B-flat3, D4, C4, A3), the chord on "et" C7 (his C), and C3 on the song's last "te!" (his A3), so the last chord has its fifth. Breaths written in for beginners: each line's last note gives up a beat (the pause on "shew!" sung for two beats and a breath; the first verse's last "O!" for one), and in the line "Our heart's joy re- cli- neth" ("Hear me, I be- seech Thee") the tune's held F4 on "cli-" gives up a beat so that "neth" comes a beat early and the breath before "In præ- se- pi- o" falls on the beat; the song's last note is held three beats, to the bar line. Accepted from the print: the tune's E4 over the bass's E3 on "es et" (Pearsall's own, in a cadence in D minor, where E is not a leading tone); bare fourths and fifths between tune and alto, and chords without a third for three singers, only on weak beats of one beat ("ci", "bi-", "Let", "our", "age", "præ-", "in", "et"; and "pi-" and "mi-", sixths without the third), and the tune's B-flat doubled an octave below on the second refrain's "pha" (one weak beat), so that the alto can reach the third of the G minor chord on "es" without moving in octaves with the bass The alto sings his F4 on "And" (not D4, which moved in octaves with the bass against its A2), and the tenor F3 on "neth" (his A3, which made fifths with the bass into "In").
licence.source: Novello's Part-Song Book (Second Series), No. 296, "In dulci jubilo. An ancient Christmas carol, by R. L. de Pearsall, Esq. (of Willsbridge)", "Arranged for Four Voices by W. J. Westbrook", with Pearsall's preface (signed R. L. P.) and the original Latin and German words (London: Novello, Ewer and Co., 1 Berners Street and 35 Poultry; undated: HathiTrust catalogues the series [188-], volumes 10 and 11 Pearsall's, catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/002445793), pp. 82 to 88, treble, alto, tenor (an octave lower) and bass with a piano part for rehearsal, Moderato, in F major (one flat), 3/2, barred in three minims and written here with a minim as one beat (3/4), in its printed key; verses 1 and 2 read from pp. 82 to 84 of the IMSLP scan (#181801, from the HathiTrust copy) at archive.org/details/imslp-dulci-jubilo-pearsall-robert-lucas/page/n0 (p. 82), n1 (p. 83) and n2 (p. 84). Pearsall's setting was first printed in London by D'Almaine and Co., its cover dated 1836 and his preface 31 January 1837 (IMSLP #887185, In_dulci_jubilo_(Pearsall,_Robert_Lucas)); that print was not opened
